concepts.name: Binary exponentiation
concepts.statement: Writing the exponent n in binary and squaring repeatedly, a^n is the product of the squares a^(2^i) for the set bits of n, so it takes O(log n) multiplications instead of O(n).

concepts.name: Binary exponentiation for any associative operation
concepts.statement: The squaring trick needs only associativity, so it applies to modular multiplication, matrix multiplication, permutation composition and other monoids, not just numbers.

concepts.name: Iterative binary exponentiation
concepts.statement: The loop version keeps a running square of a, multiplies it into the result whenever the low bit of n is set, and shifts n right; it does the same work as the recursion without call overhead.

concepts.name: Modular exponentiation
concepts.statement: Because (a*b) mod m = ((a mod m)(b mod m)) mod m, x^n mod m is computed by binary exponentiation with every multiplication reduced mod m.

concepts.name: Applying a permutation k times
concepts.statement: Raising a permutation to the k-th power by binary exponentiation of composition applies it k times in O(n log k); decomposing into cycles does it in O(n).

concepts.name: Geometric transformations as matrix powers
concepts.statement: Shifts, scalings and rotations are linear maps in homogeneous coordinates (4x4 matrices), so a nested loop of transformations is a matrix product raised to a power by binary exponentiation.

concepts.name: Counting paths of length k by adjacency-matrix power
concepts.statement: Entry (u,v) of the k-th power of the adjacency matrix counts walks of length k from u to v, computable in O(n^3 log k).

concepts.name: Binary multiplication modulo m
concepts.statement: a*b mod m without 128-bit overflow: the same doubling scheme with additions instead of multiplications gives the product in O(log b) steps.

concepts.name: Greatest common divisor
concepts.statement: gcd(a,b) is the largest k > 0 dividing both a and b, with gcd(a,0)=a.

concepts.name: Euclidean algorithm
concepts.statement: gcd(a,b) = gcd(b, a mod b) because the pairs share the same common divisors, and recursing until b = 0 yields the GCD.

concepts.name: Lame's theorem: Euclid runs in O(log min(a,b))
concepts.statement: If b < F_n the Euclidean algorithm makes at most n-2 recursive calls, with consecutive Fibonacci numbers as the worst case, so it takes O(log min(a,b)) steps.

concepts.name: Least common multiple via GCD
concepts.statement: lcm(a,b) = a*b / gcd(a,b); computing a / gcd(a,b) * b first avoids overflow.

concepts.name: Binary GCD (Stein's algorithm)
concepts.statement: Using gcd(2a,2b)=2gcd(a,b), gcd(2a,b)=gcd(a,b) for odd b and gcd(a,b)=gcd(a-b,b), the GCD can be computed with shifts and subtractions only, avoiding slow modulo.

concepts.name: Bezout's identity
concepts.statement: For integers a and b there exist integers x, y with a*x + b*y = gcd(a,b), and gcd(a,b) is the smallest positive integer of that form.

concepts.name: Extended Euclidean algorithm
concepts.statement: Back-substituting through the Euclidean recursion, from (x,y)=(1,0) at b=0 via x = y1, y = x1 - y1*floor(a/b), produces Bezout coefficients along with the GCD.

concepts.name: Iterative extended Euclid
concepts.statement: Coefficient pairs are kept as invariants a1 = a*x + b*y alongside the iterative Euclid loop, so the extended version runs without recursion.

concepts.name: Linear Diophantine equation in two variables
concepts.statement: An equation a*x + b*y = c in unknown integers x, y; a = b = 0 is degenerate (no or infinitely many solutions).

concepts.name: Solvability and one solution of ax+by=c
concepts.statement: ax+by=c has a solution iff g = gcd(a,b) divides c; scaling the extended-Euclid coefficients by c/g gives one, with sign fixes for negative a, b.

concepts.name: General solution of a linear Diophantine equation
concepts.statement: All solutions are x = x0 + k*b/g, y = y0 - k*a/g for integer k.

concepts.name: Counting Diophantine solutions in a box
concepts.statement: Shifting a solution with the general form to the bounds [minx,maxx] and [miny,maxy] and intersecting the resulting ranges of k counts and lists the solutions in the box.

concepts.name: Diophantine solution minimising x+y
concepts.statement: x+y changes by k(b-a)/g along the solution family, so the extreme is at an end of the allowed range of k.

concepts.name: Fibonacci identities
concepts.statement: Cassini's identity F_{n-1}F_{n+1} - F_n^2 = (-1)^n, the addition rule F_{n+k} = F_k F_{n+1} + F_{k-1} F_n, F_{2n} divisibility facts and gcd(F_m,F_n) = F_{gcd(m,n)}.

concepts.name: Zeckendorf representation and Fibonacci coding
concepts.statement: Every natural number is uniquely a sum of non-consecutive Fibonacci numbers (found greedily), giving a prefix code terminated by "11".

concepts.name: Binet's formula
concepts.statement: F_n = (phi^n - psi^n)/sqrt5 with phi = (1+sqrt5)/2; since |psi^n/sqrt5| < 1/2, F_n is phi^n/sqrt5 rounded, though floating precision limits its use.

concepts.name: Fibonacci in linear time
concepts.statement: Keeping only the last two values, F_n is computed in O(n) time and O(1) memory.

concepts.name: Fibonacci via matrix exponentiation
concepts.statement: [[1,1],[1,0]]^n = [[F_{n+1},F_n],[F_n,F_{n-1}]], so F_n is computed in O(log n) by binary exponentiation of a 2x2 matrix.

concepts.name: Fast doubling for Fibonacci
concepts.statement: F_{2k} = F_k(2F_{k+1} - F_k) and F_{2k+1} = F_{k+1}^2 + F_k^2 give (F_n, F_{n+1}) recursively in O(log n) with fewer multiplications than the matrix power.

concepts.name: Periodicity of Fibonacci modulo p
concepts.statement: There are at most p^2 pairs of residues, so by pigeonhole the Fibonacci sequence mod p is periodic, with period at most p^2 (the Pisano period).

concepts.name: Sieve of Eratosthenes
concepts.statement: Marking the multiples of each prime as composite, starting from its square, leaves exactly the primes in [2, n].

concepts.name: Sieve runs in O(n log log n)
concepts.statement: The work is n times the sum of 1/p over primes p <= n, which is about n ln ln n by the prime number theorem; a cruder harmonic bound gives O(n log n).

concepts.name: Sieving only by primes up to sqrt(n)
concepts.statement: Every composite <= n has a prime factor <= sqrt(n), so sieving by those primes suffices; it saves operations without changing the asymptotics.

concepts.name: Odd-only sieve
concepts.statement: Storing and sieving only odd numbers halves memory and roughly halves the work.

concepts.name: Bit-packed sieve and memory trade-offs
concepts.statement: vector<bool> or bitset stores one bit per number, cutting memory eightfold at the cost of slower bit access; which is faster depends on cache behaviour.

concepts.name: Segmented sieve
concepts.statement: Using the primes up to sqrt(n), the range is sieved block by block of size about sqrt(n), giving O(sqrt n) memory and better cache use for the same total work.

concepts.name: Primes in a range [L, R]
concepts.statement: Primes up to sqrt(R) mark composites in [L,R] directly, finding all primes in a short interval with very large R in O((R-L+1) log log R + sqrt R).

concepts.name: Linear sieve
concepts.statement: For each i, multiplying i by each found prime p <= lp[i] sets lp[i*p] = p; every composite is reached exactly once via its least prime factor, giving primes and least prime factors in O(n).
concepts.notes: No practice list. Overlaps sieve-of-eratosthenes#linear-time-modification (a pointer only).

concepts.name: Each composite is marked exactly once
concepts.statement: Writing i = lp[i]*x uniquely with lp[i] <= lp[x], the sieve visits i only from x with prime lp[i], so every lp value is set once.

concepts.name: Least prime factor table for fast factorisation
concepts.statement: The lp[] array costs more memory than a bit sieve but lets any number up to n be factored in O(number of prime factors) by repeated division.

concepts.name: Primality by trial division
concepts.statement: A composite n has a divisor d <= sqrt(n), so testing divisors up to sqrt(n) decides primality in O(sqrt n).

concepts.name: Fermat primality test
concepts.statement: If a^(n-1) is not 1 mod n for some base a, n is composite; random bases make a probabilistic test, defeated by Carmichael numbers.

concepts.name: Miller-Rabin primality test
concepts.statement: Writing n-1 = 2^s d, a prime n gives a^d = 1 or a^(2^r d) = -1 mod n for some r < s; a base violating this proves n composite, and a fixed base set (the first 12 primes) is deterministic for 64-bit n.

concepts.name: Prime factorisation by trial division
concepts.statement: Dividing out each d from 2 to sqrt(n) yields the prime factorisation in O(sqrt n); whatever remains above 1 is prime.

concepts.name: Wheel factorisation
concepts.statement: After removing small primes (2, 3, 5...), only candidates coprime to their product need testing, skipping a fixed pattern of residues.

concepts.name: Trial division by precomputed primes
concepts.statement: Sieving primes up to sqrt(n) first and dividing only by them is the limit of the wheel idea.

concepts.name: Fermat's factorisation method
concepts.statement: An odd n = pq is a difference of squares ((p+q)/2)^2 - ((p-q)/2)^2, so searching a >= sqrt(n) for square a^2 - n finds factors fast when they are close.

concepts.name: Pollard's p-1 method
concepts.statement: If p-1 is B-powersmooth for a prime factor p, then with M the product of prime powers up to B, gcd(a^M - 1, n) reveals p.

concepts.name: Pollard's rho algorithm
concepts.statement: The pseudo-random sequence x -> x^2 + c mod n cycles mod a factor p after about sqrt(p) steps, so a cycle-finding gcd(|x_i - x_j|, n) exposes p in expected O(n^(1/4)) evaluations.

concepts.name: Brent's cycle-finding in Pollard rho
concepts.statement: Advancing the reference pointer at powers of two and batching gcd computations over products of differences cuts function evaluations relative to Floyd's method.

concepts.name: Euler's totient function
concepts.statement: phi(n) counts integers in [1, n] coprime to n.

concepts.name: Totient product formula
concepts.statement: phi(p^k) = p^k - p^(k-1) and phi is multiplicative, so phi(n) = n * prod over primes p | n of (1 - 1/p).

concepts.name: Computing phi(n) by factorisation
concepts.statement: Trial-dividing n and applying result -= result/p for each distinct prime factor gives phi(n) in O(sqrt n).

concepts.name: Totients of 1..n by sieve
concepts.statement: For each prime p, every multiple has phi[i] -= phi[i]/p, giving all totients up to n in O(n log log n).

concepts.name: Gauss's divisor-sum identity
concepts.statement: Sum over d | n of phi(d) = n, which also gives an O(n log n) way to compute all totients by subtracting phi(i) from multiples of i.

concepts.name: Euler's theorem
concepts.statement: a^phi(m) = 1 mod m when gcd(a,m) = 1; consequently a^n = a^(n mod phi(m)) mod m for coprime a, m.

concepts.name: Fermat's little theorem
concepts.statement: For prime p and a not divisible by p, a^(p-1) = 1 mod p; the special case of Euler's theorem with phi(p) = p-1.

concepts.name: Exponent reduction for non-coprime bases
concepts.statement: For any x, m and n >= log2 m, x^n = x^(phi(m) + (n mod phi(m))) mod m, which lets towers of exponents be reduced mod phi(m).

concepts.name: Number of divisors formula
concepts.statement: If n = prod p_i^e_i then d(n) = prod (e_i + 1), since a divisor picks an exponent 0..e_i for each prime.

concepts.name: Sum of divisors formula
concepts.statement: sigma(n) = prod (p_i^(e_i+1) - 1)/(p_i - 1), a product of geometric series over the prime powers.

concepts.name: Multiplicative functions
concepts.statement: f is multiplicative if f(ab) = f(a)f(b) for coprime a, b; d(n), sigma(n) and phi(n) are examples, and Dirichlet convolution preserves the property.

concepts.name: Modular multiplicative inverse
concepts.statement: x is an inverse of a mod m if a*x = 1 mod m; it exists iff gcd(a, m) = 1 and is then unique mod m.

concepts.name: Inverse via extended Euclid
concepts.statement: Solving a*x + m*y = 1 with the extended Euclidean algorithm gives x mod m as the inverse, in O(log m).

concepts.name: Inverse via Fermat/Euler
concepts.statement: By Euler's theorem a^(phi(m)-1) is the inverse; for prime m this is a^(m-2) mod m by binary exponentiation.

concepts.name: Linear-time inverses of 1..m-1 mod prime
concepts.statement: From m = k*a + r, inv[a] = -floor(m/a) * inv[m mod a] mod m, which fills a table of all inverses in O(m).

concepts.name: Batch inversion with prefix products
concepts.statement: Inverting the product of all elements once and peeling off with prefix and suffix products gives every element's inverse with a single modular inversion and O(n) multiplications.

concepts.name: Linear congruence a*x = b (mod n)
concepts.statement: Find x in [0, n-1] with a*x congruent to b mod n.

concepts.name: Solving a linear congruence
concepts.statement: If gcd(a,n) = 1 the unique solution is x = b*a^-1 mod n; otherwise with g = gcd(a,n) there are no solutions unless g | b, and then exactly g solutions spaced n/g apart, from the reduced congruence.

concepts.name: Linear congruence as a Diophantine equation
concepts.statement: a*x = b mod n is a*x + n*k = b, so extended Euclid gives a solution and the Diophantine general solution gives the rest.

concepts.name: Chinese Remainder Theorem
concepts.statement: For pairwise coprime m_1..m_k, a system a = a_i mod m_i has exactly one solution mod m = m_1*...*m_k; equivalently Z_m is isomorphic to the product of the Z_{m_i}.

concepts.name: CRT for two moduli
concepts.statement: With Bezout coefficients n1*m1 + n2*m2 = 1, a = a1*n2*m2 + a2*n1*m1 mod m1*m2 satisfies both congruences.

concepts.name: Inductive CRT for many moduli
concepts.statement: Merging congruences two at a time, the product of the first i moduli being coprime to the next, solves any number of congruences.

concepts.name: Direct CRT construction
concepts.statement: a = sum a_i * M_i * (M_i^-1 mod m_i) mod m, with M_i the product of the other moduli (a Lagrange-interpolation-like formula).

concepts.name: CRT with non-coprime moduli
concepts.statement: A general system has a unique solution mod lcm(m_i) or none; two congruences are compatible iff a1 = a2 mod gcd(m1, m2), and can be merged by splitting moduli into prime powers or via extended Euclid.

concepts.name: Mixed radix representation
concepts.statement: a = x_1 + x_2 p_1 + x_3 p_1 p_2 + ... with digits x_i in [0, p_i), generalising positional number systems.
concepts.notes: No practice list. Duplicates chinese-remainder-theorem#garners-algorithm and big-integer#long-integer-arithmetic-in-prime-modulos-garner-algorithm, which summarise this article.

concepts.name: Garner's algorithm
concepts.statement: From residues a_i = a mod p_i and inverses r_ij = p_i^-1 mod p_j, the mixed-radix digits x_i are found one at a time in O(k^2), reconstructing a without big-number division.

concepts.name: Residue number system for big integers
concepts.statement: Storing a big number as residues modulo many primes makes +, - and * componentwise; Garner converts back to an ordinary integer.

concepts.name: Factorial with p-factors removed, mod p
concepts.statement: n!_%p is n! with all factors of p removed, taken mod p; it is what remains when the same p-powers cancel between numerator and denominator.

concepts.name: Computing n! mod p without p-factors
concepts.statement: The product splits into floor(n/p) full blocks, each (p-1)! = -1 mod p by Wilson's theorem, a partial block, and (floor(n/p))!_%p recursively, giving O(p + log_p n).

concepts.name: Legendre's formula
concepts.statement: The exponent of prime p in n! is the sum of floor(n/p^i) for i >= 1, computed in O(log_p n).

concepts.name: Discrete logarithm problem
concepts.statement: Find x with a^x = b mod m; a solution need not exist.
concepts.notes: Article practice list: 5 external links (#practice-problems); 2 reference links.

concepts.name: Baby-step giant-step
concepts.statement: Writing x = n*p - q, the equation becomes (a^n)^p = b*a^q mod m; tabulating one side for all p and matching the other side for all q solves it in O(sqrt m log m) with n near sqrt m.

concepts.name: Meet in the middle (as used in BSGS)
concepts.statement: Splitting an unknown into two halves and matching tabulated values of one half against the other turns an O(m) search into O(sqrt m) work and memory.
concepts.notes: cp-algorithms has no standalone meet-in-the-middle article in this scope; the idea appears only inside baby-step giant-step.

concepts.name: BSGS with incremental powers and hashing
concepts.statement: Updating powers by one multiplication per step and storing them in a hash table removes the log factors.

concepts.name: Discrete log for non-coprime a and m
concepts.statement: Repeatedly dividing out g = gcd(a, m) (checking g | b) reduces the equation to a coprime one with an extra constant factor, which BSGS still handles.

concepts.name: Primitive root modulo n
concepts.statement: g is a primitive root mod n if every number coprime to n is a power of g mod n; equivalently the multiplicative order of g is phi(n).

concepts.name: Existence of primitive roots
concepts.statement: A primitive root mod n exists iff n is 1, 2, 4, p^k or 2p^k for an odd prime p; when one exists there are phi(phi(n)) of them.

concepts.name: Finding a primitive root
concepts.statement: g is a primitive root iff g^(phi(n)/p) is not 1 mod n for every prime p dividing phi(n); testing candidates in order finds one quickly.

concepts.name: Discrete root via primitive root and discrete log
concepts.statement: For prime n, writing x = g^y with g a primitive root turns x^k = a into (g^k)^y = a mod n, a discrete log problem.

concepts.name: All discrete roots from one
concepts.statement: Since g has order phi(n), all solutions are x = g^(y0 + i*phi(n)/gcd(k, phi(n))) for integer i.

concepts.name: Montgomery representation
concepts.statement: With r = 2^k > n coprime to n, x is represented as x*r mod n; addition is unchanged and the product of representatives needs one division by r.

concepts.name: Montgomery reduction (REDC)
concepts.statement: x*r^-1 mod n is computed as (x - (x*n' mod r)*n)/r with n' = n^-1 mod r, using only multiplications, shifts and masks instead of division.

concepts.name: Inverse modulo 2^k by Newton iteration
concepts.statement: If a*x = 1 mod 2^k then a*x*(2 - a*x) = 1 mod 2^2k, so a few iterations give n^-1 mod 2^64.

concepts.name: Fast conversion into Montgomery form
concepts.statement: x*r mod n equals the Montgomery product of x and precomputed r^2 mod n.

concepts.name: Balanced ternary
concepts.statement: A base-3 positional system with digits -1, 0, 1 (written Z, 0, 1) that represents negative numbers without a sign.

concepts.name: Converting to balanced ternary
concepts.statement: From ordinary ternary, scanning from the lowest digit, a 2 becomes Z with a carry of 1 and a 3 becomes 0 with a carry.

concepts.name: Gray code
concepts.statement: An ordering of binary numbers in which consecutive values differ in exactly one bit.

concepts.name: G(n) = n xor (n >> 1)
concepts.statement: Bit i of G(n) is set exactly when bits i and i+1 of n differ, so G(n) = n ^ (n >> 1).

concepts.name: Inverse Gray code
concepts.statement: n is recovered from g by prefix xor from the top bit down: n_i = g_i xor n_{i+1}.

concepts.name: Applications of Gray codes
concepts.statement: Gray codes trace a Hamiltonian cycle on the hypercube, reduce sensor and DAC errors, and give the move order in the Towers of Hanoi.

concepts.name: Binary representation and two's complement
concepts.statement: An integer is a sum of a_i 2^i; fixed-width signed integers use two's complement, where -x = ~x + 1.

concepts.name: Bitwise AND, OR, XOR, NOT
concepts.statement: &, |, ^ and ~ act on each bit position independently; they run as fast as addition on fixed-width integers.

concepts.name: Shift operators
concepts.statement: x >> k is floor division by 2^k and x << k is multiplication by 2^k (within the word width).

concepts.name: Setting, clearing, flipping and testing a bit
concepts.statement: n | (1<<x) sets bit x, n & ~(1<<x) clears it, n ^ (1<<x) flips it, and (n >> x) & 1 reads it.

concepts.name: Power-of-two and divisibility-by-2^k tests
concepts.statement: n > 0 is a power of two iff n & (n-1) = 0, and n is divisible by 2^k iff n & ((1<<k)-1) = 0.

concepts.name: Lowest-set-bit tricks
concepts.statement: n & (n-1) clears the lowest set bit, n & -n isolates it, and n & (n+1) / n | (n+1) clear trailing ones / set the lowest clear bit.

concepts.name: Brian Kernighan's bit counting
concepts.statement: Repeatedly clearing the lowest set bit counts set bits in as many iterations as there are ones.

concepts.name: Counting set bits over 0..n
concepts.statement: Numbers below 2^x contain x*2^(x-1) ones, so the total for 0..n follows from the highest set bit recursively in O(log n).

concepts.name: Enumerating submasks
concepts.statement: s = (s-1) & m steps through all submasks of m in decreasing order, visiting 2^popcount(m) of them; the empty submask needs separate handling.

concepts.name: All masks with all submasks is O(3^n)
concepts.statement: Each bit is either absent from m, in m but not s, or in both, so iterating every submask of every n-bit mask takes 3^n steps in total.

concepts.name: Big integers as digit arrays
concepts.statement: A big integer is stored as a little-endian vector of digits in base 10^9, kept without leading zeros.

concepts.name: Schoolbook big-integer addition and subtraction
concepts.statement: Digit-wise addition with carry, or subtraction with borrow for a >= b, runs in O(n), followed by stripping leading zeros.

concepts.name: Big-integer multiplication
concepts.statement: Multiplying by a word-size integer propagates a carry in O(n); multiplying two big integers is the O(nm) schoolbook convolution with carries.

concepts.name: Big integer divided by a short integer
concepts.statement: Long division from the most significant digit, carrying the remainder times the base, gives quotient and remainder in O(n).

concepts.name: Numbers stored as prime factorisations
concepts.statement: Storing exponents of primes makes multiplication and division cheap (and suits non-prime moduli) but rules out addition.

concepts.name: Big integers as residues modulo primes
concepts.statement: Residues modulo several primes determine a number below their product by CRT; Garner's algorithm restores it.
concepts.notes: Short summary of the garners-algorithm article.

concepts.name: Exact fraction arithmetic
concepts.statement: Rationals are kept as numerator/denominator reduced by the GCD after each operation.

concepts.name: Floating point with a separate exponent
concepts.statement: Keeping the exponent in a separate integer and renormalising the mantissa avoids overflow and underflow beyond double's range.

concepts.name: Discrete Fourier transform
concepts.statement: The DFT of a degree-(n-1) polynomial is its values at the n complex n-th roots of unity.

concepts.name: Polynomial multiplication via pointwise products
concepts.statement: DFT(A*B) = DFT(A) . DFT(B) pointwise, so multiplying polynomials is a forward transform, a pointwise product and an inverse transform; big integers are polynomials in their base.

concepts.name: Fast Fourier transform
concepts.statement: Splitting A(x) = A0(x^2) + x A1(x^2) into even and odd coefficients and using w^(k+n/2) = -w^k computes the DFT by divide and conquer in O(n log n).

concepts.name: Inverse FFT
concepts.statement: The inverse DFT is the DFT with conjugated roots, divided by n, because the Vandermonde matrix of roots of unity has a scaled conjugate as its inverse.

concepts.name: In-place iterative FFT with bit reversal
concepts.statement: Permuting coefficients into bit-reversed order lets butterflies combine adjacent blocks in place, bottom up, avoiding recursion and temporary vectors.

concepts.name: Number theoretic transform
concepts.statement: In Z_p with p = c*2^k + 1 (e.g. 998244353) there are 2^k-th roots of unity, so the FFT runs exactly in modular arithmetic without rounding error.

concepts.name: Polynomial multiplication for an arbitrary modulus
concepts.statement: Splitting coefficients into high and low halves (or using three NTT primes and CRT) keeps floating-point FFT products exact for any modulus.

concepts.name: Problems reduced to convolution
concepts.statement: Counting all pairwise sums a_i + b_j, all cyclic scalar products, stripe fitting, and string matching (with wildcards) via sum (p - t)^2 p t become one or a few polynomial multiplications.

concepts.name: Formal power series
concepts.statement: An infinite sum of a_i x^i treated as a coefficient sequence regardless of convergence, with products as convolutions and work done modulo x^k.
concepts.notes: Article problem list: 4 external links (#problems). Code is an external library link, not inline.

concepts.name: Polynomial Euclidean division
concepts.statement: A = D*B + R with deg R < deg B; reversing coefficients turns finding D into a power-series inverse, giving O(n log n).

concepts.name: Power-series inverse by Newton/Hensel lifting
concepts.statement: If A(0) != 0, iterating Q <- Q(2 - A Q) mod x^(2k) doubles the number of correct coefficients of 1/A each step, for O(n log n) total.

concepts.name: Newton's method on power series
concepts.statement: For F(Q) = 0, Q_{k+1} = Q_k - F(Q_k)/F'(Q_k) mod x^(2^(k+1)) (Hensel's lemma), which yields inverse, square root, exp and other functions of a series.

concepts.name: Logarithm, exponent and powers of a series
concepts.statement: ln P = integral of P'/P; exp is found by Newton on ln Q - P; and P^k = exp(k ln P) after normalising the lowest term, each in O(n log n).

concepts.name: Multipoint evaluation and interpolation
concepts.statement: Reducing A modulo a segment tree of products (x - x_i) evaluates it at n points in O(n log^2 n); Lagrange interpolation is done in the same time by divide and conquer.

concepts.name: Chirp-z transform
concepts.statement: Evaluating at z^(2r) becomes one convolution via 2kr = r^2 + k^2 - (r-k)^2.

concepts.name: Polynomial GCD and resultant
concepts.statement: The resultant (product of A at the roots of B, scaled) is zero iff A and B share a root and can be computed by a Euclid-like recursion; half-GCD brings GCD and resultant to O(n log^2 n).

concepts.name: Continued fraction representation
concepts.statement: r = [a0; a1, ..., ak] = a0 + 1/(a1 + 1/(...)); rationals have finite expansions (two of them), irrationals infinite ones.
concepts.notes: Article practice list: 9 external links (#practice-problems); plus worked problem examples.

concepts.name: Computing a continued fraction by Euclid
concepts.statement: For p/q the next complete quotient is q/(p mod q), so the partial quotients are exactly the Euclidean algorithm's quotients.

concepts.name: Convergents and their recurrence
concepts.statement: The convergents p_k/q_k = [a0;...;ak] satisfy p_k = a_k p_{k-1} + p_{k-2} and likewise for q_k, with p_k q_{k-1} - p_{k-1} q_k = (-1)^(k-1).

concepts.name: Best rational approximation
concepts.statement: |r - p_k/q_k| <= 1/(q_k q_{k+1}) <= 1/q_k^2, alternating sides; convergents and semiconvergents are the best approximations with bounded denominator.

concepts.name: Stern-Brocot path from a continued fraction
concepts.statement: The path to p/q in the Stern-Brocot tree is a run-length encoding of its continued fraction: a0 right moves, a1 left moves and so on.

concepts.name: Calkin-Wilf tree
concepts.statement: A binary tree rooted at 1/1 where p/q has children p/(p+q) and (p+q)/q; it contains every positive rational once.

concepts.name: Linear fractional transformations
concepts.statement: Maps x -> (ax+b)/(cx+d) compose like 2x2 matrices, and a continued fraction is a composition of x -> a_k + 1/x, which gives algorithms for arithmetic on continued fractions.

concepts.name: Geometric interpretation: convex hull of lattice points
concepts.statement: Convergent vectors (q_k, p_k) alternate around the line y = r x and trace the convex hulls of lattice points above and below it, which solves floor-sum and lattice-hull problems.

concepts.name: Exponentiation mod 2^d by factoring
concepts.statement: Every x = 1 mod 4 is 5^L(x) mod 2^d, so a*x^y = a*5^(y L(x)) can be computed by writing x and 5^z as products of (2^k + 1) factors using O(d) additions and bit operations and one multiplication.

concepts.name: Logarithm table via Pohlig-Hellman for 2^d
concepts.statement: The values 4L(2^n + 1) are found bit by bit by squaring both sides k times, a Pohlig-Hellman variant for moduli that are powers of two.

concepts.name: Gauss-Jordan elimination
concepts.statement: Row swaps, scaling by non-zero numbers and adding multiples of one row to another preserve the solution set, so eliminating each variable from every other equation reduces the system to read-off form.

concepts.name: Pivot selection (partial pivoting)
concepts.statement: Swapping in the row with the largest absolute value in the current column avoids division by zero and limits floating-point error growth.

concepts.name: Detecting no, one or infinitely many solutions
concepts.statement: Columns without a pivot are free variables (infinitely many solutions if consistent); a row reduced to 0 = non-zero means no solution.

concepts.name: Complexity of Gaussian elimination
concepts.statement: Elimination takes O(min(n,m) * n * m), i.e. O(n^3) for a square system; splitting into forward elimination and back substitution halves the constant.

concepts.name: Gaussian elimination mod 2 with bitsets
concepts.statement: Over GF(2) row addition is XOR, so rows stored as bitsets eliminate 32-64 entries per word operation; any prime modulus works with modular inverses.

concepts.name: Refining the solution numerically
concepts.statement: For ill-conditioned matrices, running a simple iteration method from the Gauss-Jordan answer reduces the error.

concepts.name: Determinant by Gaussian elimination
concepts.statement: Eliminating to triangular form, the determinant is the product of the pivots times -1 per row swap, in O(n^3).
concepts.notes: Thin article (about 200 words). Article practice list: 1 external link (#practice-problems).

concepts.name: Determinant via LU (Crout/Kraut) decomposition
concepts.statement: Factoring A = L U with unit-diagonal L, det A is the product of U's diagonal; the factors are computed column by column in O(n^3).
concepts.notes: Thin article (about 245 words), no practice list.

concepts.name: Rank of a matrix
concepts.statement: The maximum number of linearly independent rows (equivalently columns), or the largest order of a non-zero minor.
concepts.notes: Thin article (about 230 words). Problem list: 1 external link (#problems).

concepts.name: Rank by Gaussian elimination
concepts.statement: Running elimination and skipping columns with no available pivot, the number of pivots chosen is the rank, in O(n^3).

concepts.name: Largest power of a prime dividing n!
concepts.statement: Every k-th factor contributes one k, every k^2-th another, so the answer is sum floor(n/k^i), computable by repeatedly dividing n by k.
concepts.notes: Thin article (about 256 words), no practice list. Duplicates factorial-modulo#multiplicity-of-p (legendre-formula).

concepts.name: Largest power of a composite k dividing n!
concepts.statement: With k = prod k_i^p_i, the answer is the minimum over i of floor(a_i / p_i), where a_i is the exponent of k_i in n!.

concepts.name: Binomial coefficient and binomial theorem
concepts.statement: C(n,k) counts k-element subsets of an n-set and is the coefficient of a^(n-k) b^k in (a+b)^n.
concepts.notes: Article practice list: 17 external links (#practice-problems); 3 reference links.

concepts.name: Factorial formula and Pascal recurrence
concepts.statement: C(n,k) = n!/(k!(n-k)!) by counting ordered selections, and C(n,k) = C(n-1,k-1) + C(n-1,k) with C(n,0) = C(n,n) = 1.

concepts.name: Binomial identities
concepts.statement: Symmetry C(n,k) = C(n,n-k), absorption C(n,k) = n/k C(n-1,k-1), row sum 2^n, hockey-stick sum over n, Vandermonde's identity and sum of squares C(2n,n).

concepts.name: Overflow-safe multiplicative computation
concepts.statement: Multiplying by (n-k+i)/i for i = 1..k keeps every intermediate value an integer (a binomial coefficient), avoiding large factorials.

concepts.name: Pascal's triangle table
concepts.statement: Filling C[n][k] by the recurrence uses only additions, never exceeds the answer and works under any modulus, in O(n^2).

concepts.name: Binomial coefficients modulo a large prime
concepts.statement: Precomputing factorials and inverse factorials mod prime m > n gives each C(n,k) in O(1).

concepts.name: Binomial coefficients modulo a prime power or arbitrary m
concepts.statement: Modulo p^b, track the exponent of p separately (Legendre) and invert the p-free factorial parts; for arbitrary m, combine prime-power results by CRT.

concepts.name: Lucas's theorem
concepts.statement: For prime p, C(n,k) mod p is the product of C(n_i,k_i) over the base-p digits of n and k; a generalisation of Lucas handles prime-power moduli.

concepts.name: Catalan numbers
concepts.statement: The sequence 1, 1, 2, 5, 14, 42, 132, ... counting many recursively defined structures.
concepts.notes: Article practice list: 7 external links (#practice-problems); 3 links in the applications list, 2 reference links.

concepts.name: Objects counted by Catalan numbers
concepts.statement: C_n counts balanced bracket sequences with n pairs, full binary trees with n+1 leaves, parenthesisations of n+1 factors, triangulations of an (n+2)-gon, monotone lattice paths not crossing the diagonal, 231-avoiding permutations and more.

concepts.name: Catalan recurrence
concepts.statement: C_n = sum over k of C_k C_{n-1-k}, from splitting a bracket sequence at the partner of its first opening bracket; O(n^2) DP.

concepts.name: Catalan closed form by reflection
concepts.statement: C_n = C(2n,n)/(n+1) = C(2n,n) - C(2n,n-1), since paths crossing the diagonal are reflected one-to-one onto paths to a shifted endpoint.

concepts.name: Inclusion-exclusion principle
concepts.statement: |A_1 u ... u A_n| = sum over non-empty J of (-1)^(|J|-1) |intersection of A_j, j in J|; the same holds for probabilities of a union of events.

concepts.name: Proof of inclusion-exclusion
concepts.statement: An element lying in k of the sets is counted sum_{i>=1} (-1)^(i-1) C(k,i) = 1 time by the formula.

concepts.name: Counting elements in exactly r sets
concepts.statement: The number of elements in exactly r of the sets is sum_{m>=r} (-1)^(m-r) C(m,r) S_m, where S_m sums the sizes of all m-wise intersections.

concepts.name: Counting via the complement of bad events
concepts.statement: To count objects satisfying every condition, count those violating at least one with inclusion-exclusion and subtract, e.g. sequences over {0,1,2} using each digit: 3^n - 3*2^n + 3.

concepts.name: Integers in [1, r] coprime to n
concepts.statement: Inclusion-exclusion over subsets of n's distinct prime factors, each term r / (product), counts numbers sharing a factor; subtract from r.

concepts.name: Lattice paths avoiding obstacles
concepts.statement: Sorting the k forbidden cells and letting d[i] be paths to cell i avoiding earlier ones (total paths minus d[j] times paths from j to i) counts paths in O(k^2) for huge grids.

concepts.name: Inclusion-exclusion over square-free divisors
concepts.statement: Counting tuples with gcd 1 by summing (-1)^(number of primes of d) times the tuples all divisible by d, over square-free d (a Mobius inversion).

concepts.name: Derangements
concepts.statement: The number of permutations with no fixed point is sum (-1)^k C(n,k)(n-k)! = n! sum (-1)^k / k!, the integer nearest to n!/e.

concepts.name: Counting objects up to symmetry
concepts.statement: Representations (e.g. colourings) are grouped into equivalence classes by a group of invariant permutations; the task is to count the classes.

concepts.name: Burnside's lemma
concepts.statement: The number of classes equals the average number of fixed points: (1/|G|) * sum over pi in G of I(pi).

concepts.name: Polya enumeration theorem
concepts.statement: A colouring with k colours is fixed by pi iff it is constant on pi's cycles, so the class count is (1/|G|) sum k^C(pi), C(pi) being the number of cycles.

concepts.name: Counting necklaces
concepts.statement: Under rotations, the shift by i has gcd(i,n) cycles, so there are (1/n) sum_i k^gcd(i,n) necklaces.

concepts.name: Burnside by generating the group programmatically
concepts.statement: When the group is too large to analyse by hand, generate it from a few basic permutations by closure, count each element's cycles, and apply Polya.

concepts.name: Stars and bars
concepts.statement: n identical objects go into k labelled boxes in C(n+k-1, n) ways: arrangements of n stars and k-1 bars.

concepts.name: Compositions into positive parts
concepts.statement: x_1 + ... + x_k = n with x_i >= 1 has C(n-1, k-1) solutions: choose k-1 of the n-1 gaps between stars.

concepts.name: Sums with lower bounds
concepts.statement: Substituting x_i' = x_i - a_i reduces lower bounds to the non-negative case, giving C(n - sum a_i + k - 1, k - 1).

concepts.name: Sums with upper bounds
concepts.statement: Upper bounds are handled by inclusion-exclusion over the variables that exceed their bound, each case reduced to stars and bars.
concepts.notes: Stub section here (a pointer); the worked version is inclusion-exclusion#number-of-upper-bound-integer-sums.

concepts.name: Next k-combination in lexicographic order
concepts.statement: Find the rightmost element below its maximum (n-k+i), increment it, and reset the following elements to consecutive values; iterating from {1..k} lists all C(n,k) subsets.

concepts.name: k-combinations with minimal change via Gray codes
concepts.statement: Taking the Gray codes with exactly k ones, or a recursive revolving-door construction, lists k-subsets so that consecutive ones differ by swapping one element.

concepts.name: Non-attacking bishops by diagonal DP
concepts.statement: Black and white diagonals are independent; sorting diagonals of one colour by length, D[i][j] = D[i-1][j] + D[i-1][j-1](d_i - j + 1), and the answer convolves the two colours.
concepts.notes: Short article (about 376 words), no practice list.

concepts.name: Balanced bracket sequence
concepts.statement: The empty string is balanced, and if s and t are balanced then so are (s) and st.

concepts.name: Checking bracket balance
concepts.statement: With one bracket type, a depth counter that never goes negative and ends at 0 suffices; with several types, a stack must match each closing bracket with the most recent unmatched opening one.

concepts.name: Number of balanced bracket sequences
concepts.statement: There are C_n = C(2n,n)/(n+1) balanced sequences of n pairs, and C_n k^n with k bracket types.

concepts.name: Next balanced sequence in lexicographic order
concepts.statement: Change the rightmost "(" that can become ")" while keeping a non-negative prefix balance, then fill the rest with the smallest completion: all "(" then all ")".

concepts.name: Generating all balanced sequences
concepts.statement: Start from ((...)) and repeatedly take the next sequence, or for small n filter permutations.

concepts.name: Index and k-th balanced sequence
concepts.statement: With d[i][j] the number of ways to finish a prefix of length i and balance j, ranking a sequence or unranking the k-th one walks character by character in O(n^2).

concepts.name: Number of labelled graphs
concepts.statement: There are 2^(n(n-1)/2) labelled simple undirected graphs on n vertices, one per subset of possible edges.

concepts.name: Number of connected labelled graphs
concepts.statement: Counting disconnected graphs by the component of vertex 1, C_n = G_n - (1/n) sum_k k C(n,k) C_k G_{n-k}, an O(n^2) recurrence.

concepts.name: Labelled graphs with k components
concepts.statement: D[n][k] = sum_s C(n-1, s-1) C_s D[n-s][k-1], choosing the size s of the component containing vertex 1.

concepts.name: Binary search in a sorted array
concepts.statement: Comparing the key with the middle element halves the candidate range each step, so a sorted array of n elements is searched in O(log n) comparisons.
concepts.notes: Practice lists: 15 external links (#binary-search_1, under the Practice Problems heading) and 2 for parallel binary search (#parallel-binary-search_1).

concepts.name: Lower bound and upper bound
concepts.statement: lower_bound(k) is the first position with A_i >= k and upper_bound(k) the first with A_i > k; together they bound the range of elements equal to k.

concepts.name: Half-open interval invariant for binary search
concepts.statement: Keeping A_L <= k < A_R (with virtual A_-1 = -inf, A_n = +inf) and shrinking until R = L + 1 avoids off-by-one errors; M = L + (R-L)/2 avoids overflow.

concepts.name: Binary search on a monotone predicate
concepts.statement: Any monotone boolean f on 0..n-1 has a single 0-to-1 boundary that binary search finds in O(log n) evaluations of f.

concepts.name: Binary search on the answer
concepts.statement: When it is easier to check "is the answer at least x?" than to compute the answer, binary search over x with that check as the predicate.

concepts.name: Bisection on real numbers
concepts.statement: For continuous f on [L, R] the intermediate value theorem guarantees a solution of f(x) = y, and halving the interval a fixed number of times (or to precision eps) finds it.

concepts.name: Binary search by descending powers of two
concepts.statement: Advance a pointer by 2^k whenever the predicate is still 0 at i + 2^k, for k from high to low; this is the form used for binary lifting and Fenwick-tree descent.

concepts.name: Parallel binary search
concepts.statement: Advance the binary searches of all queries in lockstep, one level per round, processing query midpoints in sorted order so each round shares one sweep of the data (with a Fenwick or segment tree); the meteors example runs in O((N+K) log N log K).

concepts.name: Unimodal function
concepts.statement: f increases then decreases on [l, r] (or the reverse), with a single maximum point or plateau.

concepts.name: Ternary search
concepts.statement: Comparing f at two interior points m1 < m2 rules out [l, m1] or [m2, r] for a unimodal f, so the extremum is found in O(log((r-l)/eps)) evaluations.

concepts.name: Ternary search over integers
concepts.statement: On integers, stop when r - l < 3 and check the remaining points directly; for strictly unimodal integer functions binary search on f(m) < f(m+1) also works.

concepts.name: Golden-section search
concepts.statement: Placing m1, m2 in the golden ratio lets one evaluation be reused each iteration, cutting function evaluations per step to one.

concepts.name: Newton's method for root finding
concepts.statement: x_{i+1} = x_i - f(x_i)/f'(x_i), the x-intercept of the tangent, converges quadratically near a simple root from a good start.

concepts.name: Square roots by Newton's method
concepts.statement: x_{i+1} = (x_i + n/x_i)/2 converges to sqrt(n); the integer version stops once the sequence stops decreasing, and it extends to big integers.

concepts.name: State-space optimisation with an energy function
concepts.statement: Find the state s minimising E(s) over a discrete state space with many local minima, e.g. tour length for the travelling salesman problem.

concepts.name: Neighbouring states
concepts.statement: A neighbour is produced from a state by a small random transformation, e.g. swapping two cities in a TSP tour.

concepts.name: Simulated annealing
concepts.statement: Move to a random neighbour if better; otherwise accept it with probability exp(-(E_next - E)/T) while the temperature T decays geometrically, which lets the search escape local minima.

concepts.name: Tuning temperature and decay
concepts.statement: The initial T, the decay u < 1 (slower cooling usually gives better results) and a time-based stop control the trade-off; iterations are about log(T_min/T)/log(u).

concepts.name: Composite Simpson's rule
concepts.statement: Fitting a parabola on each pair of subintervals gives the integral of f over [a, b] as (h/3)(f(x_0) + 4f(x_1) + 2f(x_2) + 4f(x_3) + ... + f(x_2n)).
concepts.notes: Short article (about 390 words). Article practice list: 1 external link (#practice-problems).

concepts.name: Error of Simpson's rule
concepts.statement: One panel has error -(1/90)((b-a)/2)^5 f''''(xi), so the composite rule is O((b-a) h^4) for bounded fourth derivative.

concepts.name: Points as vectors
concepts.statement: A point is identified with its position vector; 2D and 3D points support addition and scalar multiplication.
concepts.notes: No practice list. The "Exercises" heading holds two worked examples, not exercises.

concepts.name: Dot product
concepts.statement: a . b = |a||b| cos theta = sum a_i b_i; it is the length of a times the length of b's projection onto a.

concepts.name: Geometry with the dot product
concepts.statement: Norms, lengths, projections and angles follow from the dot product; a . b = 0 iff the vectors are orthogonal, and its sign tells acute from obtuse.

concepts.name: Cross product and triple product
concepts.statement: In 3D, a x b is the vector with (a x b) . c equal to the signed volume of the parallelepiped on a, b, c; in 2D the pseudo-scalar a x b = a_x b_y - a_y b_x is the signed parallelogram area.

concepts.name: Orientation and collinearity via cross product
concepts.statement: a x b = 0 iff a and b are collinear and the triple product is 0 iff three vectors are coplanar; the sign of the 2D cross product says whether b turns left or right of a.

concepts.name: Intersecting parametric lines
concepts.statement: Writing lines as a + t d and crossing both sides with d_2 gives t = ((a_2 - a_1) x d_2)/(d_1 x d_2).

concepts.name: Intersecting three planes
concepts.statement: Three planes r . n_i = a_i . n_i meet at a point given by Cramer's rule with triple products.

concepts.name: Line equation through two points
concepts.statement: The line through P and Q is Ax + By + C = 0 with A = P_y - Q_y, B = Q_x - P_x, C = -A P_x - B P_y.

concepts.name: Normalising integer and real line equations
concepts.statement: For integer coordinates divide A, B, C by their GCD and fix the sign to get a canonical form; for reals, normalise (A, B) to unit length and compare with a tolerance.

concepts.name: Parametric line in 3D and higher
concepts.statement: Beyond 2D a line is p + v t with v = Q - P, since no single equation describes it.

concepts.name: Intersection of two lines by Cramer's rule
concepts.statement: For a_i x + b_i y + c_i = 0 the lines are parallel iff a_1 b_2 - a_2 b_1 = 0; otherwise the point is given by Cramer's rule, with eps comparisons for reals.
concepts.notes: Thin article (about 306 words), no practice list.

concepts.name: Do two segments intersect?
concepts.statement: Collinear segments intersect iff their x- and y-projections overlap; otherwise c, d must not be strictly on the same side of line ab and vice versa, all checked with integer orientation signs.
concepts.notes: Thin article (about 167 words). Article practice list: 1 external link (#practice-problems).

concepts.name: Computing the intersection of two segments
concepts.statement: Intersect the supporting lines; if parallel and coincident the answer is the overlap of the projections (a segment or point), otherwise check that the crossing point lies on both segments.
concepts.notes: Short article (about 376 words), no practice list.

concepts.name: Circle-line intersection
concepts.statement: With the circle at the origin, the closest point of the line is (-AC, -BC)/(A^2+B^2) at distance d; there are 0, 1 or 2 points as d >r, = r or < r, the latter offset by sqrt(r^2 - d^2) along the line.

concepts.name: Circle-circle intersection
concepts.statement: Subtracting the two circle equations leaves the radical line Ax + By + C = 0, so the problem reduces to circle-line intersection (coincident circles handled separately).
concepts.notes: Thin article (about 297 words), no code. Article practice list: 7 external links (#practice-problems).

concepts.name: Number of common tangents of two circles
concepts.statement: Two circles have 0, 1, 2, 3, 4 or infinitely many common tangents depending on their relative position.

concepts.name: Finding common tangents
concepts.statement: With the first circle at the origin, a tangent ax + by + c = 0 (a^2+b^2 = 1) satisfies c = +-r1 and a v_x + b v_y + c = +-r2; solving the four sign cases gives all tangents, including point-circle tangents.

concepts.name: Length of a union of segments (Klee)
concepts.statement: Sort all endpoints, sweep with a counter of open segments, and add the gap to the next endpoint whenever the counter is positive: O(n log n), which is optimal.
concepts.notes: Thin article (about 158 words), no practice list.

concepts.name: Signed area of a triangle
concepts.statement: Half the 2D cross product (p2 - p1) x (p3 - p2) is the triangle's area, positive for counter-clockwise and negative for clockwise orientation.
concepts.notes: Thin article (about 236 words). Article practice list: 1 external link (#practice-problems).

concepts.name: Area of a simple polygon (shoelace)
concepts.statement: Summing signed trapezoids (p_x - q_x)(p_y + q_y)/2 over the edges, or signed triangles from any fixed point, gives the polygon's area; the sign gives the orientation.
concepts.notes: Thin article (about 168 words), no practice list.

concepts.name: Point in convex polygon in O(log n)
concepts.statement: From the lowest-leftmost vertex p0, the other vertices are sorted by angle; binary search finds the wedge p0 p_i p_{i+1} containing the query, then one orientation test decides inside or out.

concepts.name: Minkowski sum
concepts.statement: A + B = {a + b : a in A, b in B}; for convex polygons the sum is a convex polygon.

concepts.name: Minkowski sum of convex polygons in linear time
concepts.statement: Starting at both lowest vertices, merge the two edge sequences by polar angle (comparing with cross products); the merged edges form the sum in O(|P| + |Q|).

concepts.name: Distance between convex polygons via Minkowski sum
concepts.statement: dist(P, Q) is the distance from the origin to P + (-Q), so the polygons intersect iff the origin lies in that sum.

concepts.name: Pick's theorem
concepts.statement: A lattice polygon has area S = I + B/2 - 1, with I interior and B boundary lattice points; B is the sum of gcd(|dx|, |dy|) over the edges.

concepts.name: Proof of Pick's theorem
concepts.statement: The formula is checked for unit squares, axis-aligned rectangles and right triangles, then shown additive when gluing polygons along an edge.

concepts.name: No Pick formula in 3D (Reeve tetrahedron)
concepts.statement: Reeve's tetrahedra (0,0,0), (1,0,0), (0,1,0), (1,1,k) all have the same lattice-point counts but volume k/6, so no analogue exists in higher dimensions.

concepts.name: Lattice points under a line (floor sum)
concepts.statement: The count of points with 0 <= x < n and 0 < y <= floor(kx + b) is reduced by peeling off floor(k) and floor(b) and swapping axes, a Euclid-like recursion running in O(log n) steps.

concepts.name: Lattice points in a polygon with arbitrary vertices
concepts.statement: Summing the signed count of lattice points under each edge, as in the trapezoid area formula, counts points in a polygon whose vertices are not lattice points.

concepts.name: Convex hull
concepts.statement: The convex hull of a point set is the smallest convex polygon containing all the points.

concepts.name: Graham's scan
concepts.statement: Sort points by polar angle around the bottom-most point and sweep with a stack, popping while the last two points and the new one do not make a counter-clockwise turn: O(n log n).

concepts.name: Andrew's monotone chain
concepts.statement: Sort points by x, then build the upper and lower hulls by the same stack-and-orientation sweep, avoiding polar angles: O(n log n), with an option to keep collinear points.

concepts.name: Minimum over lines in DP transitions
concepts.statement: Transitions of the form dp_i = min_j (k_j x_i + b_j) ask for the minimum of a set of linear functions at a point, such as in the fuel-cost example.

concepts.name: Convex hull trick
concepts.statement: Treating lines as points (k, b), only those on the lower convex hull can be minimal; with slopes added in order the hull is kept on a stack and queries are answered by binary search (or a pointer for monotone x).

concepts.name: Li Chao tree
concepts.statement: A segment tree over x stores in each node the line that wins at its midpoint and pushes the loser to the one child where it can still win, giving O(log C) insertion and point-minimum query for any functions that cross at most once.

concepts.name: Detecting an intersecting pair by sweep line
concepts.statement: Sweep a vertical line over the endpoints, keep the segments it crosses ordered by y in a balanced BST, and test only neighbours on insertion and deletion; the first intersection is found in O(n log n) (Shamos-Hoey).

concepts.name: Euler's formula for planar graphs
concepts.statement: A connected planar embedding has n - m + f = 2 (n - m + f = 1 + k with k components), so m <= 3n - 6, f <= 2n - 4 and some vertex has degree at most 5.
concepts.notes: Facts stated without proof. Problem list: 2 external links (#problems).

concepts.name: Finding faces by next-edge traversal
concepts.statement: With adjacency lists sorted by angle, repeatedly leaving each vertex by the edge after the one you arrived on traces each face once; the outer face is the one traversed counter-clockwise; O(m log m).

concepts.name: Building a planar graph from segments
concepts.statement: Intersect each segment with all others, sort the points on it and connect consecutive ones, merging equal points by hashing, in O(n^2 log n).

concepts.name: Offline point location in O(log n)
concepts.statement: Sweep over x with events for edge insertions, deletions and queries, keeping edges ordered by y in a set; each query finds the edge just below it and hence its face.

concepts.name: Online point location with persistent trees
concepts.statement: Making the sweep's ordered set persistent allows queries to be answered online.

concepts.name: Closest pair of points by divide and conquer
concepts.statement: Split by median x, solve both halves, then check pairs across a strip of width 2h, merging by y; each point has O(1) candidates within h, giving O(n log n).

concepts.name: Constant candidates in the strip
concepts.statement: Points with pairwise distance at least h pack into an h x 2h rectangle only O(1) at a time, so each point is compared with a constant number of others.

concepts.name: Randomized expected-linear closest pair
concepts.statement: Guess d as the minimum of n random pair distances, hash points into d x d cells, and compare only within neighbouring cells; the expected time is O(n).

concepts.name: Minimum-perimeter triangle
concepts.statement: The same divide and conquer with strip width about minper/2 finds three points of minimum total pairwise distance in O(n log n).

concepts.name: Voronoi diagram and Delaunay triangulation
concepts.statement: The Voronoi cell of p_i is the set of points closest to p_i; a Delaunay triangulation has no input point strictly inside any triangle's circumcircle.

concepts.name: Delaunay properties and duality
concepts.statement: The Delaunay triangulation maximises the minimum angle, contains the Euclidean MST, and is dual to the Voronoi diagram (in general position), so either is found from the other in O(n).

concepts.name: Guibas-Stolfi divide and conquer Delaunay
concepts.statement: Sort points, triangulate halves recursively, and stitch them bottom-up with in-circle tests, using the quad-edge structure: O(n log n).

concepts.name: Vertical decomposition
concepts.statement: Cutting the plane by vertical lines through all vertices and intersection points leaves stripes in which shapes are trapezoids, so each stripe is solved independently.

concepts.name: Area of a union of triangles
concepts.statement: In each stripe the union is a set of disjoint trapezoids; with per-segment processing and bracket balance, the total is O(n^2 log n) time and O(n) memory.

concepts.name: Intersecting convex polygons by stripes
concepts.statement: Within each stripe two convex polygons are trapezoids, so their intersection is built stripe by stripe in linear time.

concepts.name: Half-planes as point-plus-direction
concepts.statement: A half-plane is the region to the left of a directed line given by a point and a direction vector; the intersection of half-planes is a convex region, possibly empty or unbounded.
concepts.notes: Problem lists: 6 links (#classic-problems-direct-application) and 8 links (#harder-problems); 8 reference links.

concepts.name: Incremental O(n^2) half-plane intersection
concepts.statement: Start from a bounding box and cut the convex polygon by one half-plane at a time.

concepts.name: Sort-and-incremental half-plane intersection
concepts.statement: Sort half-planes by angle and sweep with a deque, popping from the back and front while the intersection of the last two lies outside the new half-plane; with a bounding box this gives O(n log n).

concepts.name: Applications of half-plane intersection
concepts.statement: Intersecting convex polygons, finding a polygon's kernel (visibility), checking feasibility inside a binary search (largest inscribed circle), and two-variable linear programming.

concepts.name: Manhattan distance
concepts.statement: d(p, q) = |x_p - x_q| + |y_p - y_q|, the taxicab metric; its ball is a diamond.

concepts.name: Farthest pair in Manhattan distance
concepts.statement: Maximising over the 2^(d-1) sign patterns of +-x +-y, the answer is the max over patterns of (max - min) of the signed sums: O(n 2^d).

concepts.name: Rotating Manhattan into Chebyshev distance
concepts.statement: |m| + |n| = max(|m+n|, |m-n|), so mapping (x, y) to (x+y, x-y) turns Manhattan distance into Chebyshev distance.

concepts.name: Manhattan minimum spanning tree
concepts.statement: Some MST uses only edges from each point to its nearest neighbour in each of 8 octants, so O(n) candidate edges found by sweeps and Kruskal give the MST in O(n log n).

concepts.name: Minimum enclosing circle
concepts.statement: The circle of minimum radius containing all given points; it is determined by two or three of them.

concepts.name: Welzl's randomized algorithm
concepts.statement: Shuffle the points; whenever p_i lies outside the current circle, rebuild with p_i on the boundary, nesting up to three levels; expected O(n) by backward analysis.

concepts.name: In-circle tests for 2- and 3-point circles
concepts.statement: z is inside the circle with diameter ab iff angle azb is not acute; for the circumcircle of abc, compare signed angles azb and bca, all exactly with complex-number arithmetic.

concepts.name: Range minimum query problem
concepts.statement: Answer queries min(A[L..R]) on an array, possibly with updates; it also underlies LCA.
concepts.notes: Index page (about 361 words) that only lists approaches in other articles. Article practice list: 3 external links (#practice-problems).

concepts.name: Choosing an RMQ structure
concepts.statement: With updates: sqrt decomposition O(sqrt n) or segment tree O(log n); static: sparse table O(1) after O(n log n), sqrt tree, disjoint sparse table, Farach-Colton-Bender O(1) after O(n), or offline DSU / Arpa.

concepts.name: Maximum subarray sum problem
concepts.statement: Find l <= r maximising a[l] + ... + a[r] for an array that may contain negative numbers.

concepts.name: Maximum subarray via prefix sums and running minimum
concepts.statement: The best sum ending at r is s[r] - min_{l<r} s[l], so one pass keeping the minimum prefix sum solves it in O(n).

concepts.name: Kadane's algorithm
concepts.statement: Accumulate a running sum, reset it to 0 whenever it becomes negative, and track the maximum value seen; O(n) time and O(1) space.

concepts.name: Maximum-sum submatrix
concepts.statement: Fixing a pair of rows and running Kadane on the column sums gives O(n^3).

concepts.name: Maximum-average subarray with a length bound
concepts.statement: Binary search on the average x, subtracting x from every element and checking for a subarray of length at least L with non-negative sum.

concepts.name: Quickselect for the k-th order statistic
concepts.statement: Partition around a pivot as in quicksort and recurse into the side containing position k only; with random pivots the expected time is O(n).
concepts.notes: Thin article (about 195 words). Practice list: 2 external links (#practice-problems); notes mention median of medians and std::nth_element.

concepts.name: Deterministic linear selection
concepts.statement: Median of medians gives a worst-case O(n) pivot; std::nth_element provides selection in C++.

concepts.name: MEX of a sequence
concepts.statement: mex(A) is the smallest non-negative integer not in A; for |A| = N it is at most N.

concepts.name: Computing MEX in O(N)
concepts.statement: Mark values below N in a boolean array (ignoring larger ones) and scan for the first unmarked index.

concepts.name: MEX under point updates
concepts.statement: Keep counts of values 0..N in a segment tree (or a set of missing values) and descend to the first zero count, giving O(log N) per update.

concepts.name: Win/lose/draw on arbitrary game graphs
concepts.statement: Starting from known terminal positions, a vertex is winning if some move leads to a losing vertex and losing if all moves lead to winning ones; a reverse-edge BFS/DFS with out-degree counters labels all vertices in O(m), and the unlabelled ones are draws.

concepts.name: Policeman and thief game
concepts.statement: Positions (policeman cell, thief cell, whose turn) form the game graph, which retrograde analysis solves.

concepts.name: Impartial games
concepts.statement: Two-player, perfect-information, finite acyclic games where available moves depend only on the position, and the player unable to move loses.
concepts.notes: Article practice list: 7 external links (#practice-problems). No code.

concepts.name: Nim: winning iff the xor of pile sizes is non-zero
concepts.statement: From a non-zero xor some move makes it zero, and from zero every move makes it non-zero (Bouton), so the first player wins iff the xor is non-zero.

concepts.name: Misere Nim
concepts.statement: Play as in normal Nim until every pile is at most 1, then leave an odd number of single-stone piles.

concepts.name: Nim with increases
concepts.statement: Allowing piles to grow (keeping the game acyclic) does not change winning positions, since an increase can be undone.

concepts.name: Sprague-Grundy theorem
concepts.statement: Every impartial game position is equivalent to a Nim pile of size mex of the Grundy values of its successors; the position is losing iff its Grundy value is 0.

concepts.name: Grundy values of sums of games
concepts.statement: A position that splits into independent games has Grundy value equal to the xor of the parts' values.

concepts.name: Finding patterns in Grundy tables
concepts.statement: Tabulate Grundy values by brute force and look for periodicity, then prove it by induction.

concepts.name: Single-machine scheduling with linear penalties
concepts.statement: Swapping adjacent jobs shows that with penalties c_i t the optimal order sorts jobs by t_i / c_i (Smith's rule).

concepts.name: Exponential and identical penalty cases
concepts.statement: With c_i e^(alpha t) sort by (1 - e^(alpha t_i))/c_i; with one shared increasing penalty sort by processing time.

concepts.name: Livshits-Kladov theorem
concepts.statement: The adjacent-exchange permutation method works only for linear, exponential and identical-monotone penalty functions.

concepts.name: Johnson's rule for two-machine flow shop
concepts.statement: To minimise makespan when every job runs on machine 1 then machine 2, put jobs with a_i <= b_i first in increasing a_i, then the rest in decreasing b_i: O(n log n).

concepts.name: Maximum number of jobs meeting deadlines
concepts.statement: Process deadlines in decreasing order, push each job into a priority queue keyed by duration, and fill each gap down to the next deadline with the shortest remaining jobs, running the last one partially and returning its remainder to the queue; O(n log n).
concepts.notes: Thin article (about 309 words), no practice list.

concepts.name: Floyd's cycle detection (tortoise and hare)
concepts.statement: Move one pointer one step and another two steps at a time; they meet iff the linked list has a cycle, within O(length) steps.
concepts.notes: Problem list: 4 external links (#problems). Also taught in factorization#floyds-cycle-finding-algorithm for Pollard rho.

concepts.name: Finding where the cycle starts
concepts.statement: After the pointers meet, reset one to the head and advance both one step at a time; they meet at the cycle's first node.

concepts.name: Why the reset finds the cycle start
concepts.statement: With a steps to the cycle and length L, the meeting point satisfies a + b = (y - 2x)L, so walking a more steps from it lands on the cycle start.

concepts.name: Josephus problem
concepts.statement: n people in a circle, every k-th is removed; find the last one remaining.

concepts.name: Josephus recurrence in O(n)
concepts.statement: In 0-indexing, J(n,k) = (J(n-1,k) + k) mod n with J(1,k) = 0.

concepts.name: Josephus in O(k log n) for small k
concepts.statement: Remove floor(n/k) people in one pass, recurse on the rest and map the index back, giving O(k log n).

concepts.name: Closed form for k = 2
concepts.statement: J(2n) = 2J(n) - 1 and J(2n+1) = 2J(n) + 1 (1-indexed), so J(n) = 2(n - 2^floor(log2 n)) + 1: a left rotation of n's binary digits.

concepts.name: Solvability of the 15 puzzle
concepts.statement: With N the number of inversions among the tiles and K the row of the blank, a position is solvable iff N + K is even.
concepts.notes: Short article (about 366 words). Article practice list: 1 external link (#practice-problems).

concepts.name: Stern-Brocot tree
concepts.statement: Starting from 0/1 and 1/0 and repeatedly inserting the mediant (a+c)/(b+d) between neighbours builds a binary search tree containing every positive rational exactly once, in lowest terms.

concepts.name: Ordering, irreducibility and completeness
concepts.statement: The mediant lies between its parents, neighbours satisfy bc - ad = 1 (so every fraction is reduced), and a search for any p/q terminates, so every positive rational appears.

concepts.name: Stern-Brocot path as a number system
concepts.statement: Comparing with the mediant and going left or right writes p/q as an L/R string; the naive search can take O(p+q) steps.

concepts.name: Logarithmic Stern-Brocot search
concepts.statement: Taking runs of a same-direction steps at once (computing a by division) reduces the search to O(log(p+q)), the same as computing the continued fraction.

concepts.name: Farey sequences
concepts.statement: F_n is the sorted list of reduced fractions in [0, 1] with denominator at most n; each interior term is the mediant of its neighbours.

concepts.name: Length of a Farey sequence
concepts.statement: |F_n| = |F_{n-1}| + phi(n) = 1 + sum_{k<=n} phi(k).
